questions.prompt: What should the first pass do for this clockwise-rotation approach?

choices.label: Swap every off-diagonal pair twice, once from each row containing it.
choices.feedback: Transposing exchanges row and column coordinates; swapping a pair twice would undo that change.

choices.label: Transpose the matrix across its main diagonal, swapping each pair once.
choices.feedback: Transposing exchanges row and column coordinates; swapping a pair twice would undo that change.

choices.label: Reverse all columns first and keep each row in its original order.
choices.feedback: Transposing exchanges row and column coordinates; swapping a pair twice would undo that change.

questions.prompt: What should follow the transpose to complete a clockwise quarter-turn?

choices.label: Reverse every row.
choices.feedback: Reversing rows after transposing places each original column into its clockwise-rotated row.

choices.label: Reverse every column.
choices.feedback: Reversing rows after transposing places each original column into its clockwise-rotated row.

choices.label: Transpose across the main diagonal again.
choices.feedback: Reversing rows after transposing places each original column into its clockwise-rotated row.

questions.prompt: What should “n” store after this step?

choices.label: Option A
choices.feedback: This stores “0” in “n”. On this test, it returns [[3,2,1],[6,5,4],[9,8,7]]; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

choices.label: Option B
choices.feedback: Set “n” to the length of “matrix”.

choices.label: Option C
choices.feedback: This stores “(len(matrix)) - 1” in “n”. On this test, it returns [[3,4,1],[6,5,2],[9,8,7]]; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

choices.label: Option D
choices.feedback: This stores “(len(matrix)) + 1” in “n”. On this test, it raises IndexError: list index out of range; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

questions.prompt: Which values should “i” visit, and in what order?

choices.label: Option A
choices.feedback: This uses “for i in list(range(n))[1:]:” instead of “for i in range(n):”. On this test, it returns [[3,2,1],[8,5,4],[9,6,7]]; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

choices.label: Option B
choices.feedback: This uses “for i in []:” instead of “for i in range(n):”. On this test, it returns [[3,2,1],[6,5,4],[9,8,7]]; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

choices.label: Option C
choices.feedback: Start “i” at 0, change it by 1 each time, and stop before “n”.

questions.prompt: Which values should “j” visit, and in what order?

choices.label: Option A
choices.feedback: Start “j” at “i” plus 1, change it by 1 each time, and stop before “n”.

choices.label: Option B
choices.feedback: This uses “for j in range((i - 1), n):” instead of “for j in range(i + 1, n):”. On this test, it returns [[3,2,1],[6,5,4],[9,8,7]]; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

choices.label: Option C
choices.feedback: This uses “for j in list(range(i + 1, n))[1:]:” instead of “for j in range(i + 1, n):”. On this test, it returns [[7,2,1],[6,5,4],[9,8,3]]; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

choices.label: Option D
choices.feedback: This uses “for j in range((i % 1), n):” instead of “for j in range(i + 1, n):”. On this test, it returns [[3,2,1],[6,5,4],[9,8,7]]; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

questions.prompt: What should “matrix[i][j], matrix[j][i]” store after this step?

choices.label: Option A
choices.feedback: This stores “matrix[j][i], matrix[i][j]” in “matrix[i][0], matrix[j][i]”. On this test, it returns [[3,2,7],[6,5,8],[9,6,3]]; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

choices.label: Option B
choices.feedback: This stores “matrix[j][i], matrix[i][j]” in “matrix[i][-1], matrix[j][i]”. On this test, it returns [[7,2,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,4]]; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

choices.label: Option C
choices.feedback: Swap “matrix[i][j]” and “matrix[j][i]”.

choices.label: Option D
choices.feedback: This stores “matrix[j][i], matrix[i][j]” in “matrix[i][(j) + 1], matrix[j][i]”. On this test, it raises IndexError: list assignment index out of range; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

questions.prompt: Which values should “row” visit, and in what order?

choices.label: Option A
choices.feedback: Visit each item from “matrix”, storing it as “row”.

choices.label: Option B
choices.feedback: This uses “for row in list(matrix)[1:]:” instead of “for row in matrix:”. On this test, it returns [[1,4,7],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]]; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

choices.label: Option C
choices.feedback: This uses “for row in []:” instead of “for row in matrix:”. On this test, it returns [[1,4,7],[2,5,8],[3,6,9]]; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

choices.label: Option D
choices.feedback: This uses “for row in list(matrix)[:-1]:” instead of “for row in matrix:”. On this test, it returns [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[3,6,9]]; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

questions.prompt: How should the order of “row” change?

choices.label: Option A
choices.feedback: This uses “pass” instead of “row.reverse()”. On this test, it returns [[1,4,7],[2,5,8],[3,6,9]]; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

choices.label: Option B
choices.feedback: Reverse the order of “row”.

choices.label: Option C
choices.feedback: This uses “row.reverse(); row.reverse()” instead of “row.reverse()”. On this test, it returns [[1,4,7],[2,5,8],[3,6,9]]; the expected result is [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].
